title: Abu al-Fadl, Has the Night Grown Long or Has My Patience Failed?
intro: Yaqut records that al-Tihami settled in Ramla and served as its preacher. His son was born and died there. The father addresses the child by his kunya, Abu al-Fadl, as though he could still share the bewilderment of a sleepless night. A crescent that never grew full, an eyelid that cannot close and the scent left on an empty hand give the loss a bodily presence. When he finally answers those who would stop his tears, he counts his youth and his power to bear loss among the things that have gone with his son.

translation: Abu al-Fadl, has the night grown long, or has my patience failed,
making me think the stars have ceased to move?
1.sharh: He opens by talking to the very person whose answer he has lost. A man awake all night can ordinarily measure the passing hours by the stars. Tonight even that clock fails him.

translation: I see white Ramla darkened since you went.
My lifetime is a night that opens on no dawn.
2.sharh: The colour attached to the city's name makes its darkening especially perceptible. He enlarges a sleepless night into the whole stretch of life still before him.

translation: Only because there lies in it a treasure held in trust
whose Lord will let none reclaim it till the Gathering.
3.sharh: The boy is a deposit entrusted to the soil. A deposit ordinarily comes back on request, but its true owner has fixed the day of resurrection for its return.

translation: My life for a crescent I had hoped would wax full.
Fate overtook it at the month's first light.
4.sharh: The crescent is already lovely but gives a father reason to expect still more. Fate intervenes precisely when its appearance promises a whole month ahead.

translation: And for a lion cub we hoped would grow a lion,
dead before ever drawing blood with fang or claw.
5.sharh: Fang and claw measure a power the child never had time to use. The broken expectation belongs to a wider “we” here, as though a household too had pictured his future.

translation: God's decree came to him in a land of strangers.
My life for him, a stranger in descent, in grave, in worth.
6.sharh: The parents' home lies elsewhere, so both descent and burial make the child a stranger. The third kind of strangeness belongs to his singular worth in his father's eyes.

translation: I make him bear the weight of earth, though I
would fear for him the weight of an ant's footfall.
7.sharh: He has had to do with his own hands what tenderness made unthinkable. The almost weightless foot of a tiny ant sets the scale for the unbearable load of earth.

translation: I entrust him to the dust, no safe keeper of him.
But one evil has led on to another.
8.sharh: The grave receives what he most wants to protect, yet he knows what earth does to a body. Death has compelled a second act of surrender.

translation: By God, if I could, I would share death with him.
We would die together, or he would share my years.
9.sharh: He imagines a bargain with two possible settlements. Sharing the boy's death would keep them together in death, sharing the father's remaining years would keep them together in life.

translation: But our souls belong to another.
I have no say over mine or his.
10.sharh: The imagined bargain falls outside a father's powers. Even his own life is held on terms he cannot alter, much less offer to someone else.

translation: The days have only called in what they gave.
Why did they not call it in before it filled my breast?
11.sharh: He concedes the days' right to collect their own gift. His grievance concerns the due date, after the gift had had time to occupy his whole heart.

translation: Before his love and familiar presence ran
through my heart like water in a fresh green branch.
12.sharh: Affection has entered by slow circulation. The moisture in a living branch can no longer be removed as though it were simply lodged in a vessel.

translation: I knew grief on the day I covered his body
and went home with half a soul, the other half in the grave.
13.sharh: Only one body goes into the earth, but the father who walks home feels divided. Grief becomes something a bystander could almost measure by counting who went and who returned.

translation: I know that fortunes lie in wait
to take my whole, as once they took my half.
14.sharh: Misfortunes become watchers at an ambush. The earlier loss of half his life now reads like advance notice that the rest will be claimed.

translation: Death folded him away as a cloak is folded.
His old haunts hold nothing of him but remembrance.
15.sharh: The verb for folding returns in the word for a cloak. What once occupied space has been put away, though his familiar rooms still furnish the mind with memories.

translation: Under compulsion he gave the last of his blood,
he who never used to give under compulsion.
16.sharh: Death wrings one last gift from a generous boy. The bitterness lies in compulsion itself, since his ordinary way of giving had always been free.

translation: If I weep, close kinship has a claim on my tears.
If I endure, I would preserve the promised reward.
17.sharh: Both courses have a claim. Tears honour the bond of kinship, while forbearance safeguards the religious reward promised for enduring a loss.

translation: What I bear for him brings my strength low,
yet I was fashioned, as the noble are, for patience.
18.sharh: He distinguishes a disposition acquired or built into him from what it takes to withstand this particular loss. The force that weakens him is real even in a nature schooled to endure.

translation: What patience can a mourner have whose heart's wing
flutters between breastbone and throat?
19.sharh: The heart has a wing but no room to fly. Its movement under the bones of chest and throat makes visible the physical cost of the composure others expect.

translation: He turns a sleepless eye this way and that, as though
it had no lashes to fold over it, no eyelid's rim.
20.sharh: The eye rolls from side to side. Failure to sleep feels like an anatomical loss, as if the very apparatus with which it could close had vanished.

translation: Tears cover its pupil. It looks like
a drowning man with deep seas rising over him.
21.sharh: Arabic calls the pupil the eye's “person”. Once the tears cover it, the little person inside the eye can be imagined as a man drowning at sea.

translation: Every day my sleep and waking are troubled
by his image travelling at night, his memory running on.
22.sharh: The child's image has the freedom of a night traveller. In daylight the task passes to remembrance, so waking offers no release from the interrupted sleep.

translation: Remembering him expands my breast with a sigh,
and that very breadth makes my breast tighter.
23.sharh: A deep sigh physically opens the chest. The movement that gives the lungs more space is the outward sign of inward constraint.

translation: They said, “Others' sorrows will console him.”
I answered, “Can one ember put another out?”
24.sharh: His comforters expect a common loss to lighten a private one. In his reply both griefs retain their heat when brought together.

translation: Does a gaping wound heal with another wound?
No. It spreads and runs the deeper.
25.sharh: After fire he tries the body as a test of their advice. A second wound supplies no closing edge to the first and only gives the damage room to spread.

translation: If only this consolation in another's loss would break even,
neither easing sorrow there nor feeding it.
26.sharh: He would settle for getting back from consolation exactly what he brought to it. Breaking even would be better than this steady increase of pain.

translation: Ask me no patience over him. I buried
my heart with him, and my patience lay folded inside it.
27.sharh: The people who demand patience are asking him for an object he can locate precisely. It went inside his heart, and the heart went into the grave.

translation: If you are not my heart, you are half of it,
cut from me as a crescent is cut from the full moon.
28.sharh: The crescent from the opening returns in a different relationship. This time the father is the full moon from which the shape of the smaller moon has been cut.

translation: O blessing that came and went before I had
paid God the thanks I owed for it.
29.sharh: Addressing the boy as a blessing makes his stay feel as brief as a visit. Gratitude remains an unsettled debt even after the gift itself has gone.

translation: May God your Lord grant you peace. If you
have crossed to the next life, we are on the bridge.
30.sharh: The dead child has completed a crossing. The survivors already stand on the bridge, which places them in motion towards him even as they say farewell.

translation: We are only horses in one race.
He went a little ahead. We follow in his tracks.
31.sharh: From the bridge he moves to a racecourse. The apparent gap between living and dead shrinks to a slight lead on a track they share.

translation: We raced, and the finish of our running
was death. The untried colt came first.
32.sharh: The winner is the youngest and least tried animal in the field. That odd distinction makes sense only once the finishing post is named as death.

translation: Death erased you from the sight of my eyes. It never erased
your image from my heart, your memory from my thoughts.
33.sharh: Erasure reaches one faculty and stops. Sight loses the actual figure, while inward vision and recollection keep different kinds of access to the boy.

translation: Whatever else I forget, however great its worth,
you will be in my mind for as long as I live.
34.sharh: He allows even important matters to slip away. The child's place in memory rests on a bond that survives changes in the order of everything else he values.

translation: From a time whose stroke hit you and missed me
I am on guard, lest the next one find me.
35.sharh: Time appears as a marksman who has missed one of two people standing together. Surviving the first shot is precisely what makes the father watch for the next.

translation: You left, and those you left behind you
stayed back with sorrows, worry and thought.
36.sharh: Leaving and being left are said more than once, as though the sentence itself were reluctant to move on. The departing child's legacy to the household is a new daily occupation in sorrow.

translation: If earth cast you up again, you would say
those inside it looked like those on its back.
37.sharh: Earth has a belly and a back. Grief has made the living on its surface so deathlike that the child, emerging from below, might recognise them as his counterparts.

translation: One difference only remains between us.
We feel the touch of hurt. You do not feel it.
38.sharh: Appearance made the two groups interchangeable. Sensation divides them again, leaving awareness of the injury entirely with those who survive.

translation: I placed my hopes in you for this world and, first, for faith.
I went away with a hand empty of both hopes.
39.sharh: He remembers the two futures he had imagined for his child, giving faith priority. Returning empty-handed turns disappointed expectations into something his hand can register.

translation: I visit you out of honour and devotion. In decay
one such as you is occupied beyond my faithfulness or care.
40.sharh: The visit continues to express the father's devotion. Decay claims the child's whole attention in this imagined exchange, leaving the visitor to sustain both sides of the relationship.

translation: He came after my hair was grey. I counted him
the equal of fresh youth. Blessed was that time.
41.sharh: The child arrived late in the father's life. His birth allowed his father to experience a second youth at the very point when grey hair announced the end of the first.

translation: I said, “My son's youth is mine.”
The gift simply passes from one half of me to the other.
42.sharh: The old and the young man are two halves of a single life. Youth can pass between them, which gives the earlier image of a soul cut in half a history before the funeral.

translation: He went as youth had gone. Both went
beloved and missed, leaving sweet memories and scent.
43.sharh: Child and youth leave in much the same fashion. Their good name and the sweetness of their memory acquire a scent just before ambergris appears in the next line.

translation: His stay was like dark ambergris.
He left, and the scent of perfume clung to my hand.
44.sharh: One can put down a piece of ambergris and still smell it on the fingers. The empty hand from the earlier verse now holds the one trace that absence has made perceptible.

translation: May I have broken love's pledges if, after him, I taste
forgetfulness. To forget is kin to betrayal.
45.sharh: He uses the form of an oath against himself. Consolation, understood here as ceasing to feel the loss, would make him a relative of the traitor.

translation: How can I be faithful when I have lived on after him?
An admission can speak better than an excuse.
46.sharh: The mere fact that he has survived becomes his accusation against himself. Confession offers a form of faithfulness still open to him when no explanation can satisfy his own standard.

translation: Grief enough that I called and he did not answer.
His silence came neither from composure nor from deafness.
47.sharh: The unanswered call takes us back to the opening address. Two almost identical Arabic words offer explanations a living child could have given, dignified reserve or impaired hearing.

translation: Nor was it distance that kept him silent.
Only two cubits, by measure, lie between us.
48.sharh: The final imaginable obstacle is distance. Two cubits are scarcely the span of a conversation, but measured earth can mark an absolute separation.

translation: We vie for this world's wealth, deceived, when
the utmost its riches reach is poverty.
49.sharh: The father's loss opens into a judgement on possessions. At the supposed summit of accumulation the owner must relinquish everything, so wealth carries its own impoverishment ahead of it.

translation: In this world we are passengers on a ship.
We seem to stand still while time carries us on.
50.sharh: On board a vessel the passengers remain in place relative to one another. The father's image explains how the journey to death can continue through an apparently ordinary, motionless day.

translation: I folded the nights away. The nights are stages
towards a term that travels to me as I travel on.
51.sharh: Each completed night is another stage covered. The destination itself is coming to meet him, so the distance closes from both ends.

translation: I used up days whose passing used me up.
What consumes and what is consumed both reach their term.
52.sharh: He acts on the days in one clause and undergoes their action in the next. The repeated verb makes it impossible to speak of spending time without reckoning what time spends.

translation: To God I complain of what I keep hidden.
I miss you as water is missed in barren country.
53.sharh: God can receive the grief he keeps within. Water in a wilderness is a measure of need, bringing a bodily urgency to words that might otherwise sound like a conventional farewell.

translation: Just when I passed forty and took the downward slope,
the stars of grey shone in the darkness of my hair.
54.sharh: His sense of decline has a stated starting point, beyond forty. The stars that seemed unable to move in the opening now appear as bright hairs in the darkness on his head.

translation: You who blame me, stop. My burning grief
has made my case for tears.
55.sharh: The people proposing consolation are now addressed as reprovers. His defence is the grief the poem has already made tangible, rather than a fresh argument about proper mourning.

translation: When my son has gone, my youth has gone,
and my endurance too, farewell to time.
56.sharh: The same verb carries son, youth and power of consolation away in turn. The final greeting to time is a leave-taking, spoken by someone who has lost the reasons he had for looking forward.

1.1.1-2.head: أَبو الفَضل
1.1.1-2.meaning: Abu al-Fadl, the dead child's kunya or familiar name in the form “father of Fadl”.

1.2.6.head: سَرى
1.2.6.meaning: Travel by night, used of the stars by whose motion a watcher marks the hours.

2.1.2-3.head: الرَّملَة البَيضاء
2.1.2-3.meaning: Ramla, the Palestinian town where the poet lived and his son was buried. Its whiteness gives point to the ensuing darkness.

2.2.4.head: أَفضى
2.2.4.meaning: Leads through into something, as the end of night normally opens into dawn.

3.1.6.head: وَديعَة
3.1.6.meaning: A deposit put in another's keeping until it can be returned, here the child entrusted to earth.

3.2.6.head: الحَشر
3.2.6.meaning: The Gathering of the resurrected on the Last Day, the date fixed for restitution.

4.1.1.meaning: “With my life”, an offer of one's own life as ransom for someone dear.

4.2.4-5.head: غُرَّة الشَّهر
4.2.4-5.meaning: “The month's first light”, its beginning when only a slender crescent shows.

5.1.1.head: شِبل
5.1.1.meaning: A lion cub, giving the child an adult strength he could have grown into.

5.1.5.head: غَضَنفَر
5.1.5.meaning: Ghadanfar, a name for a powerful, fully grown lion.

6.1.5-6.head: دار غُربَة
6.1.5-6.meaning: “A land of estrangement”, Ramla as a place away from the family's original home.

6.2.5.head: القَدر
6.2.5.meaning: Worth or standing, called strange in the sense of being exceptional.

7.2.5-6.head: مَوطِئ الذَّرّ
7.2.5-6.meaning: “An ant's footfall”, the pressure of tiny ants, virtually the least weight imaginable.

8.1.2.head: غَبراء
8.1.2.meaning: The dust-coloured earth, here the soil enclosing the body.

8.1.1.head: أَودَعَ
8.1.1.meaning: Place in trust with someone, recalling the earlier deposit left in the soil.

9.1.3.head: أَسطاعَ
9.1.3.meaning: Can or have the power, a shortened form of the ordinary Arabic verb for being able.

9.1.5.meaning: Death or destruction, imagined as a share the father could take upon himself.

10.1.3-4.head: مِلك غَيرِنا
10.1.3-4.meaning: “Another's possession”, God's ownership of lives which people cannot exchange at will.

10.2.5-6.head: ما فيهِ
10.2.5-6.meaning: “Nor any say over him.” The reciter repeats ma to negate the father’s power over the boy. Both printed diwans have wa-la fihi.

11.1.2.head: اِقتَضى
11.1.2.meaning: Called in or collected what was due, as a creditor collects a debt.

11.1.5.head: هِبَة
11.1.5.meaning: Gifts freely bestowed, among which the father counts the life of his son.

12.1.6.head: إِلف
12.1.6.meaning: The familiarity of continually sharing someone's company.

12.2.6.head: النَّضر
12.2.6.meaning: Fresh and flourishing, here of a branch still supplied with moisture.

13.1.5-6.head: وارى شَخصَه
13.1.5-6.meaning: “I covered his figure”, buried the body that had been visible to the father.

14.1.4.head: مَرصَد
14.1.4.meaning: In a place of ambush, lying in watch until one can strike.

14.2.5.head: شَطر
14.2.5.meaning: My half, a portion of the father's own self identified with the boy.

15.1.3-4.head: طَيّ الرِّداء
15.1.3-4.meaning: “The folding of a cloak”, gathering away something once spread out before the eye.

15.2.1.head: مَغنى
15.2.1.meaning: The dwellings and familiar places where he used to be found.

16.1.3.head: قَسر
16.1.3.meaning: Compulsion, set against the boy's habit of giving of his own accord.

16.1.5.head: دَم
16.1.5.meaning: His blood, the last thing left to give. Both diwans have dhama’ihi, the final remnant of life in a dying creature.

17.2.4.head: بُقيا
17.2.4.meaning: Preservation, here the wish to safeguard the reward promised to those who endure.

18.1.4.head: أَهوى
18.1.4.meaning: Brings his strength down. The Alexandria text has yuhi, “weakens”, and al-Rabi' prints yuni, “wearies or slackens”.

19.2.4.head: التَّرائِب
19.2.4.meaning: The bones across the upper chest towards the collarbones.

19.2.5.head: النَّحر
19.2.5.meaning: The base of the throat where it meets the upper chest.

20.2.2.head: هُدب
20.2.2.meaning: Eyelashes, the hairs growing from the eyelid.

20.2.6.head: شَفر
20.2.6.meaning: The rim of the eyelid itself, distinguished from the lashes growing on it.

21.1.3.head: إِنسان العَين
21.1.3.meaning: “The person of the eye”, the pupil, in which an observer can see a tiny reflection.

21.2.4.head: لُجَّة
21.2.4.meaning: Deep masses or swells of water heaving above the drowning person.

22.2.1.head: خَيال
22.2.1.meaning: The apparition or inward image of an absent person, particularly in sleep.

23.1.4.head: اِدِّكار
23.1.4.meaning: Recollection of him, the grammatical subject that expands the father's chest.

23.1.3.head: زَفير
23.1.3.meaning: A long, audible exhalation arising from distress.

24.1.3-4.head: التَّأَسّي بِغَيرِه
24.1.3-4.meaning: Taking consolation from the example of someone else who has suffered a similar loss.

25.1.1.head: اِندَمَلَ
25.1.1.meaning: Closes or heals, of a wound whose edges come together.

25.1.3.head: الرَّغيب
25.1.3.meaning: Wide and deep, describing a gaping wound.

25.2.5.head: اِستَشرى
25.2.5.meaning: Spreads and grows more dangerous, as disease works through tissue.

26.2.1.head: كَفاف
26.2.1.meaning: An exact balance, with neither gain in comfort nor increase in grief.

26.2.6.head: أَغرى
26.2.6.meaning: Incites or aggravates, here inciting grief to greater intensity.

27.2.5.head: طَيّ
27.2.5.meaning: Inside its folds, the innermost place where patience was kept.

28.2.1.head: قُدَّ
28.2.1.meaning: You were cut or cleft from a whole, like one shape of the moon from another.

28.2.6.head: البَدر
28.2.6.meaning: The full moon, here the undivided form from which the crescent is cut.

29.1.3-4.head: حَلَّ وَوَلّى
29.1.3-4.meaning: “Alighted and departed”, presenting a blessing as a visitor with only a short stay.

29.2.1.head: قَضى
29.2.1.meaning: Discharged or paid what was owed. Al-Nahari says qadaytu. Both printed diwans read nahadtu, “I rose to fulfil” my duty of thanks.

30.2.3.meaning: The other life, the hereafter across the bridge of this world.

31.1.6.head: حَلبَة
31.1.6.meaning: A field of racehorses or the course on which they are brought together.

31.2.4-5.head: عَلى الإِثر
31.2.4-5.meaning: “On the track”, following close behind one who has gone ahead.

31.2.1.head: تَقَدَّمَ
31.2.1.meaning: He went ahead of us. The boy is the subject and “us” the object, both carried in this one word.

32.2.5-6.head: الجَذَع الغَمر
32.2.5-6.meaning: “The untried colt”, a young animal without experience, standing for the son.

33.1.4-5.head: رَأي عَيني
33.1.4-5.meaning: “My eye's seeing”, physical sight as distinct from the inward image.

34.2.5-6.head: عَلى ذِكر
34.2.5-6.meaning: Kept in mind, continually present to one's recollection.

35.1.5.head: صَرف الدَّهر
35.1.5.meaning: “A turn of time”, a reversal descending on someone like a stroke.

36.2.2.head: حُزن
36.2.2.meaning: The plural “sorrows”, the many forms bereavement takes among the survivors.

37.1.2-3.head: لَفَظَتِ الأَرض
37.1.2-3.meaning: “The earth spat you out”, reversing burial by imagining the ground as a mouth.

37.2.4.head: بَطن الأَرض
37.2.4.meaning: The earth's belly, its buried interior as opposed to the surface on which the living stand.

38.2.1-2.head: مَسّ الأَذى
38.2.1-2.meaning: “At the touch of harm”, the sensation by which the living know pain has reached them.

39.2.5.head: صِفر
39.2.5.meaning: Empty-handed, of a palm from which both hopes have slipped.

40.1.5.meaning: The wasting or decomposition of the body in the grave.

41.1.5.head: عَدَلَ
41.1.5.meaning: Counted one thing the equal of another or its equivalent in worth.

41.2.3.head: الغَضّ
41.2.3.meaning: Tender and fresh, like a shoot still full of moisture.

42.2.2-3.head: شَطر
42.2.2-3.meaning: One half, here either of the two lives between which youth can pass.

43.2.5.head: النَّشر
43.2.5.meaning: Fragrance carried abroad, with the suggestion of a good name left behind.

44.1.3-4.head: العَنبَر الجَون
44.1.3-4.meaning: Dark ambergris, an aromatic material whose scent lingers after handling.

44.2.5-6.head: عَبَق العِطر
44.2.5-6.meaning: The trace of scent clinging to a surface after the perfume itself has gone.

45.2.1.head: سُلُوّ
45.2.1.meaning: Forgetful consolation, the fading of grief and attachment to the dead.

46.2.1-2.head: رُبَّ اِعتِراف
46.2.1-2.meaning: “Many an admission”, introducing the thought that a confession may speak better than an excuse.

47.2.5.head: وَقار
47.2.5.meaning: Dignified reserve, a possible motive for choosing silence.

47.2.7.head: وَقر
47.2.7.meaning: Deafness or impaired hearing, close in sound to the preceding word for composure.

48.2.4.head: ذِراع
48.2.4.meaning: Two cubits, each approximately the length from the elbow to the hand, measuring the depth of burial.

49.2.1.meaning: The ultimate limit or outcome of a course of striving.

50.1.4-5.head: رَكب سَفينَة
50.1.4-5.meaning: “Passengers aboard a ship”, stationary relative to the deck although the whole vessel travels.

51.1.4.head: مَرحَلَة
51.1.4.meaning: Stages of a journey between halts, each identified with a night of life.

52.2.6.head: قَدَر
52.2.6.meaning: An appointed measure or end, the term to which the process runs.

53.1.5.head: أَجَنَّ
53.1.5.meaning: Conceal or carry unspoken in the heart.

53.2.6.head: القَفر
53.2.6.meaning: Desolate, uninhabited country where water is a condition of survival.

54.1.5.head: مُصَوِّب
54.1.5.meaning: Heading downhill, an image for passing the perceived summit of life.

54.2.5-6.head: ظُلَم الشَّعر
54.2.5-6.meaning: “The darknesses of the hair”, the old black colour in which white hairs shine like stars.

55.1.3.head: لَوّام
55.1.3.meaning: Persistent reprovers who blame him for continuing to weep.

55.2.2.meaning: A burning ache kept within the breast, of longing or grief.

56.2.2.head: عَزاء
56.2.2.meaning: My power to bear or be consoled for a loss.
